item.title: Subsidize people, not things. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
If poor people don't have enough money, then the solution is to give some money to the poor people. Then they will have more money and so, depending upon how much we give them, the poor people will have enough money.
This is a simple solution which, sadly, all too much of politics refuses to understand.
This is also the solution that the World Bank insists would be right for Bangladesh .
Give the subsidy, the money, to the poor people. Don't subsidize a thing that some poor people use or need. Because people who are not poor will also get that subsidy on that thing. The way to make sure that the subsidy actually goes to those who are poor is to subsidize poor people, not things.
For example, there's a subsidy for fertilizer. But there are rich farmers as well as poor ones. As it happens, rich farmers -- because they're rich -- tend to have more land than poor ones. More land means more fertilizer use. So, richer farmers get more of the fertilizer subsidy than poorer ones do -- they use more of the subsidised fertilizer.
There are subsidies for electricity and those too are captured by those richer than the very poorest. The very poor use less electricity because they're very poor. It's richer people who have more electricity consuming equipment, so it's richer people who get more of the electricity subsidy.
That's not what we're trying to do with these subsidies. We want to make the poor better off. But any, and every, system of subsidy of things will suffer from the same problem. So, the answer is simple: Do not subsidize things, subsidize people.
Poverty relief should -- should, note -- mean giving money to poor people. Not constructing systems of subsidy for things.
There are other problems with the subsidy of things. India's system of subsidized rations for the very poor each month is well known for never actually reaching the relevant people: It's all been stolen, or gone rotten, long before it reaches them.
But there's another, more theoretical problem. Not everyone wants the same thing. For example, we have poor people who are not farmers. So, the money we spend upon fertilizer subsidies is still public money being spent upon poverty alleviation, but it is irrelevant for the poor who are not farmers. Or, say, poor people who have managed to buy a little solar power set up. Subsidizing electricity does little for them.
Perhaps they would like that subsidy to arrive in some different manner such as help with schooling costs. Or school uniforms. Or medical care. Or transport. Being poor means there's a whole parcel of things we might consider necessities that you cannot have.
The subsidy of a thing means that politicians, or bureaucrats, or even us in a democracy, are making the choice for those poor people of what will make their lives better.
But it's a central belief of any sort of liberalism that each individual knows best what makes their own life better.
Giving them money to then spend on what they want improves their life better than giving them a subsidy on what we think they might want.
This is not something restricted to the poor. It's true of the United States right now. Most of the American system of poverty alleviation is giving poor people things. Healthcare, or vouchers for food, or vouchers to pay the rent, or a free/cheap cellphone, and on and on it goes.
Very little of that US system is just giving poor people cash. As the US census itself admits -- though you have to read fairly deeply to find it -- this makes everyone in the US poorer than they need be.
The poor value these things at less than the cost of providing these things. The poor would rather have the money, then spend that on the things that they, themselves, think makes their lives better.
We must be honest about this. It is their lives and so their opinion of what makes their life better is the only correct, or even useful, one.
We can make everyone richer by simply giving people money. For any given rise in the standard of living of the poor, as determined by those poor people, it costs less money if we just give them the cash.
Equally, for whatever amount of money we use to subsidize the poor, we increase their living standards more by just giving them the cash.
We can all have the most lovely arguments about who should be subsidized. It might even be that the answer is no one. We can similarly have arguments about how much the subsidy should be.
But it simply is true that we gain the most effect for however much money we spend upon subsidies by not trying to subsidize goods, or services, but by just giving more money to poor people.
Or, as the World Bank means but doesn't quite say -- they have to be polite -- we should subsidize people, not things. Just give poor people cash.

item.title: We need cheaper flights, not more planes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
I was indulging in a favourite Bengali pastime, watching a late-night talk show with my father, when the discussion turned to Bangladesh Biman’s plans to buy more aircraft.
The guests lamented Bangladesh’s reliance on foreign airlines, with travelers connecting through overseas hubs to reach their destinations. Their prescription was more planes of our own.
Missing from the discussion were private Bangladeshi airlines. They are ours, too. If there is substantial unmet demand, as officials claim , the government should examine what keeps private carriers from serving it.
My recent US-Bangla ticket from Chittagong to Dhaka offered one place to start. The base fare was Tk2,924. Taxes, fees, and an airline surcharge added Tk1,625, bringing the total to Tk4,549.
My ticket listed these various charges as codes. A National Skills Development Authority ticketing guide helped decode them.
IMG_5626
Passengers should pay for the airport facilities and security they use, through transparent fees tied to efficient service costs.
A broad consumption tax also has a different justification from selectively taxing flying. But the excise and travel taxes alone added Tk900, or 30.8% of the base fare.
Where did this extra tax bill come from?
The Excises and Salt Act gives the government authority to levy excise duties on specified domestic services. Fixed passenger duties take the same amount from a cheap ticket as an expensive one. An airline can cut its fare, but the duty stays put, taking a larger share of the lower price.
The government piles taxes onto tickets, discouraging sales or squeezing margins that could help finance private expansion.
Then it guarantees borrowing for Biman. The public gets a double whammy: Passengers pay more today, while taxpayers bear the risk if guaranteed debt goes unpaid. Before underwriting more aircraft, the government should reduce the tax burden and let airlines test whether passengers will support the expansion.
If officials want passengers to choose Bangladeshi airlines over foreign carriers, they should begin by making it easier for private Bangladeshi airlines to compete.
Reducing the ticket-tax burden would be one place to start: Local carriers have warned that higher duties depress demand.
These ticket taxes apply to Biman too. But government-backed borrowing changes who bears the risk of expansion.
When lenders expect the state to cover a shortfall, they have less reason to scrutinize whether new routes will pay. Managers face weaker pressure to make those investments earn their keep.
A guarantee can make aircraft easier to finance without making them commercially worthwhile. Government backing can keep resources committed to an airline that would otherwise have to improve, restructure, or relinquish them to a better operator.
Boeing has confirmed 25 aircraft ordered this year; Airbus announced ten more on October 7 .
Bangladesh may need additional capacity. Biman should still demonstrate which routes justify the investment, how debt will be repaid, and whether leasing or competing carriers could provide service more economically.
For the initial 14 Boeing aircraft, the US ambassador announced US Export-Import Bank financing. A sovereign guarantee has also been reported.
If Biman defaults on guaranteed payments, the state must meet its obligations, adding pressure for taxes, borrowing or cuts to other priorities.
CPD’s FY2026-27 budget analysis lists roughly Tk6,257 crore in Biman-related guarantees. That is contingent exposure, not an annual subsidy check or a valuation of these new orders.
If Biman fails to repay the guaranteed debt, the government must pay. Whatever it cannot recover from Biman becomes a loss for taxpayers.
What can be done?
Commercial expansion should depend on passengers buying tickets and investors accepting the risk. Before asking taxpayers to back more seats, the government should make existing seats easier to buy.
It should not impose taxes simply because it can. Each levy needs an economic justification that accounts for the costs it imposes.
Revana Sharfuddin is a research fellow at the Mercatus Centre at George Mason University.

They’re not lying. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
If a person’s story changes in the weeks following an alleged sexual assault, are they not telling the truth?
It’s a criticism I’ve seen on social media and heard in the public conversation surrounding the lawsuit filed in September 2026 by a plaintiff known as Jane Doe, a former student at Cornell University, accusing seven male students of rape.
Initially, Doe discussed events with a friend but reportedly didn’t identify them as assault. It wasn’t until weeks later, when her experience was labeled as a gang rape by others, that she came forward to authorities.
Survivors are often questioned about how they relay their stories. When societal expectations about how rape survivors should respond do not align with the victim’s experience, it’s easy to assume that the victim is lying and the assailant is innocent.
Research indicates 60% to 70% of female rape survivors do not identify their experience as rape. That’s especially true for college students.
Instead, rape survivors often describe their experience in more general terms, referring to it as “bad sex” or “miscommunication.”
That’s both because of how sexual assault affects a survivor’s mind, brain, and body and because of how society thinks about rape.
In my experience as a psychologist doing crisis intervention work with rape and sexual assault victims, it is very common for survivors to prefer to continue as if the assault never happened and to be driven by a strong desire to return to normalcy.
While this seems counterintuitive, understanding the biological and psychological survival processes that sexual assault can activate may help explain why this response is perfectly logical.
Trauma’s immediate impact
Immediately following a rape, survivors -- whether they characterize their experience as rape or not -- often experience myriad symptoms broadly referred to as rape trauma syndrome.
These symptoms include self-blame, emotional dysregulation, and feelings of fear and humiliation. These symptoms often lead to problems with sleep, headaches, muscle tension, and fatigue.
Psychologists generally diagnose symptoms consistent with rape trauma syndrome as acute stress disorder. Acute stress disorder reflects the unique psychological reactions immediately following trauma, whereas the longer-term effects are characterized as post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD.
People with acute stress disorder experience at least nine symptoms across several categories, including avoidance of trauma reminders, persistent negative mood, and dissociation -- defined as a disconnection between thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations.
Other symptoms include intrusive experiences like nightmares or flashbacks, feeling like they are re-experiencing the trauma, constantly being on high alert, and having overly intense emotional reactions to reminders of the traumatic event.
The brain on trauma
During acute stress, the brain shifts into survival mode.
Two of the main bodily systems activated during this period are the limbic system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. The limbic system controls emotions, memory, and behaviour. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis controls how the body responds to stress by regulating hormones like cortisol.
These systems mobilize the body’s key survival responses -- fight, flight, freeze, and fawn.
When the limbic system and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis kick in following trauma, the internal commotion that ensues takes over the brain’s ability to control thinking, planning, and decision-making.
This effectively prevents the brain from making accurate sense of what happened and from coping with the trauma in a healthy way.
Self-blame and denial are protective
For rape survivors, a common outcome of this neurobiological storm is self-blame -- a tendency to hold themselves responsible for the events that led to the trauma.
Generally, people believe they live in a world that feels safe and predictable, and they tend to adhere to the just world hypothesis, which posits that good things happen to good people.
To preserve the illusion of control, safety, and predictability, survivors blame themselves in an effort to restore order to a world that has been incredibly shaken by trauma.
Rape survivors often experience hindsight bias -- the belief that they should have been able to predict or prevent an assault.
This belief, which further reinforces self-blame, is fortified by a culture in which rape prevention programs tend to focus on women as opposed to men, leading women to believe they alone are responsible for and can prevent rape.
Then there’s denial, a defense mechanism that can take the form of avoidance of or dissociation from the trauma.
Because the reality of what has happened is overwhelming to the brain and psyche, denying or ignoring it provides a defense from the flood of emotion that follows trauma and helps reestablish a sense of stability.
Common rape stereotypes -- for example, that rape is mainly committed by strangers in a novel situation, not by acquaintances during everyday experiences -- reinforce these feelings. In fact, statistics indicate that 80% to 90% of women are raped by someone they know.
Judging a changing story
A person assessing the reactions of a rape and trauma survivor generally does so in a calm and collected frame of mind. Yet the actions they are judging were made under extreme duress.
For a survivor of rape, an inability to clearly name the assault for what it was is a common outcome of the biological and psychological factors at play during acute stress.
This denial functions to preserve their identity and sanity during acute stress, restore order to their world and help them make rational sense of what has happened to them.
Breaking through these self-preservation mechanisms often takes time -- time that observers too often misinterpret as a false accounting of what actually happened.
Michele Patterson Ford is Senior Lecturer in Psychology, Dickinson College. This article previously appeared in The Conversation and is being reprinted under a Creative Commons-Attribution/No Derivatives license.

item.title: Afghanistan skipper Rahmat Shah thwarts Bangladesh in Abu Dhabi Test. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Skipper Rahmat Shah hit a fighting unbeaten 84 to foil Bangladesh’s bowling attack as Afghanistan reached 211-4 on the second day of the one-off Test in Abu Dhabi on Saturday.

Rahmat stood tall on a dry and hot day against some probing pace and spin to bring Afghanistan within 135 runs of Bangladesh’s first innings total of 346 at Sheikh Zayed Stadium.

Bangladesh resumed on 317-8 but managed just 29 runs in the first session.

Rahmat added a useful 70 runs for the third wicket with Abdul Malik, who scored a patient 62, after opener Sediqullah Atal fell for 17 and Shahidullah Kamal managed 20.

At close, Rahmat was unbeaten after batting for 186 balls while wicket-keeper Ikram Alikhil was 26 not out.

Bangladesh’s pace attack of Hasan Mahmud and Ebadot Hossain gave their team early breakthroughs by removing Atal and Kamal before Rahmat found an able ally to avoid further losses.

Malik matched his skipper shot for shot, hitting a six and four fours in his maiden Test half-century, finally falling to Ebadot to leave Afghanistan 134-3.

Five runs later, spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz had former skipper Hashmatullah Shahidi stumped by Litton Das for a duck.

Rahmat and Alikhil defied the bowling in the final session during their unbroken fifth-wicket stand of 72, boosting hopes of a first innings lead.

Hossain was the pick of Bangladesh’s bowlers with 2-50.

Earlier, Bangladesh’s last two wickets survived just 8.2 overs before they were bowled out for 346.

Mohammad Saleem finished with 4-82 while fellow fast bowlers Yamin Ahmadzai (3-79) and Ismat Alam (2-20) also chipped in with useful wickets.

item.title: Carrying the world upon your shoulders. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
“I’m alright. I’m okay.”
We say it with such ease. Sometimes we mean it, sometimes it is simply the answer we have learned to give while carrying worry, fatigue, or loneliness we cannot quite put into words.
Behind a casual “I’m fine” may be someone trying hard to hold everything together, someone who needs to be heard but fears being judged.
When our body hurts, we seek treatment. But when our mind struggles, too many of us remain silent.
In Bangladesh, this resounding silence meets a deficiency of care. The 2018-19 National Mental Health Survey found that 18.7% of adults and 12.6% of children aged 7-17 experienced mental health conditions.
Reported treatment gaps exceeded 92% for adults and 94% for children. Behind these figures are people and families navigating distress with little professional help.
Resources remain painfully limited. A WHO-supported report published in 2025 noted that mental health received just 0.44% of Bangladesh’s total health budget in 2021 , with two-thirds of that spending directed towards mental health hospitals. Care closer to home needs far greater investment.
We need services that people can reach, afford, and trust. Our experience points to three priorities.

This cannot be a singular effort. The government, private sector, and civil society all have to act in concert.
And each of us can begin with a small act of kindness: Ask how someone is doing, then make time for the answer.
We owe people a world where “I’m struggling” can be spoken without shame and met with compassion, dignity, and care.
Zahida Fizza Kabir is a social entrepreneur and CEO at SAJIDA Foundation.

item.title: Our roads need better planning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The inauguration of Bangladesh’s first dedicated cycle track in Chittagong is a welcome step towards safer, more sustainable urban transport. Stretching 2.2 kilometres, the new facility demonstrates how road infrastructure can be designed to accommodate cyclists and pedestrians alongside motorized traffic.
However, this initiative must be the beginning of a broader shift in how we plan our roads.
In Bangladesh, road planning has long prioritized the movement of motor vehicles, often at the expense of pedestrians, cyclists, and public transport users. In crowded cities such as Dhaka and Chittagong, this imbalance contributes to congestion, unsafe journeys, and an urban environment that discourages walking and cycling.
Dedicated cycling or bike lanes should, therefore, be introduced across major urban roads wherever feasible, with physical barriers and clear markings to prevent other vehicles from encroaching on them.
Equally important are dedicated bus lanes that allow public transport to move efficiently without being trapped in the same congestion as private cars.
Better bus services, reliable schedules, and safe boarding facilities would encourage more people to choose public transport, reducing the number of private vehicles on the roads.
These measures must be supported by comprehensive planning, and road projects must also account for drainage, roadside activity, and connections between different modes of transport instead of treating each development as an isolated undertaking.
The authorities must ensure that these facilities are maintained, kept free from illegal parking and encroachment, and supported by consistent enforcement of traffic laws.
Chittagong’s new cycle track offers a practical example of what better road design can achieve. The challenge now is to replicate -- and also improve upon -- this approach nationwide.
Our roads should not merely move vehicles faster; they must enable everyone to travel safely, comfortably, and affordably. Better road planning must be treated as a necessity for a safer, more liveable Bangladesh.

item.title: India's 'cockroach' movement chief detained ahead of major protest. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Indian police detained the head of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online movement on Saturday ahead of a major protest it called against the Election Commission, the party said.

Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital New Delhi, where the demonstration was due to take place, the youth-led CJP said in a social media post.

India deployed thousands of police in its capital and restricted transportation in and around Delhi ahead of mass demonstrations on Saturday demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over alleged voter-roll irregularities.

The protests, called by the youth-led CJP, are the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision.

Demonstrations erupted across the country after a newspaper investigation last month alleged misconduct by the Election Commission of India (ECI).

The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety in the “special intensive revision”, saying it was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters.

Opposition parties and critics say the exercise could disenfranchise voters to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the usual government-designated protest site.

Police have not authorised rallies at the site this weekend.

The protests, called by the CJP, are widely seen as a reprise of its mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal.

This time, they are demanding ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar resign.

‘Cannot detain the movement’

The allegations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office.

Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi.

However, the Supreme Court on Friday said some trains must still run and that there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.

“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on X.

“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”

The CJP, which emerged online as a satirical political movement in May, has accused authorities of intimidating its supporters ahead of the demonstration.

The party has said that “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.

Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.

Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.

“You can detain the people — you cannot detain the movement,” said Neha Bora, who has emerged as a leading face of the current protest.

The voter list overhaul, which began in 2025, has led to more than 133 million names being excluded from draft rolls.

The exclusions include duplicate entries and people found to have died.

The poll body said the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from casting ballots.

Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

item.title: Mental health is health. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, serves as an important reminder that mental health deserves more attention.
In Bangladesh, however, it remains an issue that is too often discussed in whispers, dismissed as weakness, or ignored until a crisis makes it impossible to overlook.
This silence must end if we are serious about building a healthier nation.
The pressures of modern life are taking a toll on people across all age groups. Financial insecurity, academic expectations, workplace stress, family conflicts, and uncertainty about the future can affect anyone.
Yet, many people in Bangladesh hesitate to seek help because they fear judgement, social stigma, or being misunderstood.
Mental health struggles are frequently met with advice to remain strong, pray harder, or simply move on, as though distress can be overcome through willpower alone.
Changing this reality requires sustained action. Mental health education must become a part of schools and workplaces, helping people recognize distress and understand when professional support is necessary. Affordable counselling and psychiatric services must be made more accessible, particularly outside major cities.
The government must also invest in trained professionals, strengthen community-based services, and ensure that mental healthcare receives adequate funding and policy attention.
Equally important is the role of families, educators, employers, and the media in creating environments where people can speak without fear of ridicule or discrimination. Seeking help must be treated as a responsible decision, not a source of shame.
This World Mental Health Day should be more than an annual observance marked by statements and awareness campaigns. It should encourage lasting changes in how we understand and respond to psychological distress.
It is time we accept this simple truth: Shying away from mental health issues will never create a healthy nation. We must start talking, listening, and acting -- before silence causes further harm.

item.title: Beyond physical relief. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The global theme for World Hospice and Palliative Care Day 2026, “Pain Management: An Essential Part of Palliative Care,” highlights one of the most profound challenges in modern healthcare: Preventing avoidable suffering and preserving human dignity at every stage of illness.
Pain relief is a fundamental component of compassionate care and a recognized human right. However, in countries like Bangladesh, the challenge extends beyond clinical knowledge -- it involves accessibility, awareness, healthcare infrastructure, cultural understanding, and the ability to provide care that addresses not only disease but also the person experiencing it.
As palliative care practitioners understand, textbooks and clinical guidelines teach us how to assess pain, prescribe analgesics, and manage physical symptoms. Yet, they cannot fully capture the emotional reality of sitting beside a person facing a life-limiting illness.
The deepest lessons often emerge from patients and families -- their courage, their fears, their hopes, and their unwavering desire for comfort and companionship. True palliative care begins when scientific knowledge meets human compassion.
In advanced illnesses such as cancer, pain is rarely limited to physical sensation alone. Dame Cicely Saunders’ concept of “ total pain ” transformed our understanding of suffering by recognizing that pain includes biological, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions.
A patient may experience physical discomfort, fear of death, anxiety about family responsibilities, financial distress, loneliness, or questions about meaning and purpose. Medicines can control physiological pain, but only compassionate communication, emotional support, and human presence can address the deeper layers of suffering.
This understanding is particularly important in Bangladesh, where the burden of non-communicable diseases continues to increase.
According to WHO estimates, non-communicable diseases account for approximately 63% of all deaths in Bangladesh, with conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, chronic respiratory disease, and diabetes contributing significantly to mortality.
As the population ages and chronic illnesses become more prevalent, the need for accessible palliative care services is expected to rise substantially.
As per the WHO, Globally, approximately 56.8 million people require palliative care every year, yet only about 14% of those in need receive such services. The majority of this unmet need exists in low- and middle-income countries, including Bangladesh, where healthcare systems often prioritize curative treatment while symptom control and end-of-life support remain underdeveloped.
Bangladesh has made meaningful progress in establishing palliative care services. The Department of Palliative Medicine at Bangladesh Medical University has played a pioneering role in developing institutional and community-based palliative care initiatives. Bangladesh published its National Palliative Care Guideline in 2019, marking an important step toward integrating palliative care into the national healthcare framework.
However, significant challenges remain, including limited trained professionals, inadequate public awareness, insufficient community-based services, and barriers to essential pain medicines.
One of the most critical challenges is access to appropriate pain medication, particularly opioid analgesics such as morphine, which are essential for managing moderate to severe cancer pain.
Evidence from Bangladesh has shown that restricted availability and concerns regarding opioid use have historically contributed to inadequate pain control among patients with advanced cancer.
A study examining morphine use in advanced cancer patients in Bangladesh found that limited access to morphine remained a major barrier to effective pain management, resulting in unnecessary physical suffering and emotional distress for both patients and families.
However, pain management must never be viewed only through the lens of medication. The essence of palliative care lies in restoring dignity and preserving identity when cure is no longer possible.
Dr Harvey Max Chochinov’s work on dignity therapy demonstrated that maintaining a patient’s sense of meaning, identity, and personal value can significantly reduce existential suffering near the end of life.
In Bangladeshi society, where family bonds and spiritual values hold deep importance, the role of family presence becomes especially meaningful.
A gentle touch, sitting beside a loved one, listening without judgment, offering reassurance, or sharing a prayer can provide a level of comfort that medicine alone cannot achieve. These simple acts communicate a powerful message: “You are not alone; you are still valued and loved.”
For many families, end-of-life experiences become lasting memories. Research on communication and bereavement has shown that compassionate conversations, emotional availability, and meaningful interactions between patients, caregivers, and healthcare professionals influence how families process loss. The quality of care provided during the final stages of life can shape memories that remain long after death.
Bangladesh now stands at an important point where palliative care must move beyond specialized hospital units and become integrated into primary healthcare, home-based services, and community health systems.
Training more doctors, nurses, and healthcare workers in pain assessment, symptom management, communication skills, and ethical decision-making is essential.
The WHO emphasizes that palliative care should be incorporated into healthcare systems as a core component of universal health coverage, ensuring that patients receive relief from physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering.
Ultimately, World Hospice and Palliative Care Day 2026 reminds us that pain management is not complete when pain scores decrease; it is complete when a person feels heard, respected, and accompanied.
Modern medicine can control symptoms, but compassion gives meaning to care. In the final chapters of life, patients may forget the names of medicines, procedures, and machines, but they remember the presence of those who stood beside them.
For Bangladesh, strengthening palliative care is a reflection of our collective humanity. By combining evidence-based pain management with emotional support, cultural sensitivity, and family-centered care, we can ensure that no person faces serious illness in unnecessary suffering but instead experiences comfort, dignity, and peace.
Sumit Banik is a public health activist and trainer.

item.title: Not just a naughty child. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Clinical practice can be challenging in Bangladesh, and more so if you are a psychiatrist. Your patient cries, shows anger and signs of distress.
And here you are, sitting with a curious face and non-judgmental attitude and trying to understand the explicit and implicit issues with the patient.
So, when a child of seven years entered my chamber, took two highlighters just to throw them away, jumped on the bed just to get down immediately, and ran amok, I was worried whether the child might get hurt.
I was curious, however, about the attitude of the parents. “Doctor, my child simply does not listen. He cannot sit still, does not concentrate on his studies, and is constantly getting complaints from school. He is just a naughty kid.”
For many parents and clinicians alike, this is a familiar story. A child who is constantly moving, interrupts others, forgets instructions, or struggles to complete schoolwork may quickly be labelled as “naughty,” “lazy,” “stubborn,” or “undisciplined.”
Parents fail to recognize it for what it is, and ultimately, children are subjected to repeated scolding or even physical punishment in an attempt to correct their behaviour.
But in some cases, these behaviours may reflect a neurodevelopmental condition known as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD.
ADHD is not simply about being “too active.” It is a condition in which difficulties with attention, impulse control, and/or hyperactivity are persistent and developmentally inappropriate, and they interfere with everyday functioning.
At the same time, it is important to remember that not every active or inattentive child has ADHD. A child who occasionally loses concentration during homework does not necessarily have ADHD.
Children naturally have variations in attention, energy, and behaviour. However, when difficulties persist over time, occur in more than one setting such as home and school, and significantly interfere with learning, relationships or daily functioning, professional assessment may be warranted.
There is another important reason not to jump to conclusions. Sleep problems, anxiety, depression, learning difficulties, family stress, and excessive screen use can also affect a child's attention and behaviour. A proper assessment therefore requires more than simply checking a list of symptoms.
Calling a child “bad” or giving a “smack” does not teach self-control. It may instead damage the child's confidence and relationship with parents and teachers. Children with attention or behavioral difficulties often benefit more from clear expectations, predictable routines, positive reinforcement, and appropriately structured tasks.
For example, instead of yelling at a child, parents can set a specific and realistic goal: “For the next 15 minutes, let's complete these two pages.” Breaking larger tasks into smaller steps can make them easier to manage.
Schools also have an important role. Leadership, communication, discipline, and ultimately their world view is largely shaped by how they interact at school.
A child who repeatedly leaves his seat or fails to complete assignments should not automatically be treated as a disciplinary problem. Clear and brief instructions, reasonable breaks, structured classroom routines, and positive feedback may help such children participate more effectively.
A child’s problem must be communicated with their parents without labels; labelling will automatically make parents more frustrated in an already tiring battle.
Treatment is multi-faceted. Depending on the child's needs, it may involve behavioral interventions, parent-focused strategies, educational support and, when clinically appropriate, medication.
The goal is not simply to make a child “quiet.” The goal is to improve attention, self-regulation, learning, and overall functioning.
Most importantly, an ADHD diagnosis does not mean that a child's future is determined by the disorder. With appropriate assessment, support and treatment, children with ADHD can develop their abilities and lead productive and fulfilling lives.
So, the most important change we need is a change in the question we ask. Instead of asking, “Why is this child so naughty?” we should sometimes ask: “What is making this child struggle, and what kind of help does the child need?”
Understanding the reason behind a child's behavior may be the first step toward changing that child's future.
Dr Imdadul Magfur is a psychiatrist and psychotherapist, Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College and Hospital.
